design: Designed anew from the rules in src/sim/sword.c and the open fencer art's frame counts. Each guard covers only its own line for 2 ticks; a step back holds the guard while giving 12 pixels. A slash is slow (6 ticks, the cut on tick 4, the body open while the blade is raised, time to read and parry it) and moves the bar twice as far as a lunge, which is quick (4 ticks, a 10 pixel step in before the point lands). Reach pays for the weight the rules give heavy blades: the rapier strikes from 30 pixels, the longsword and cutlass only from 4 and 3 (one more at the easiest level, where a hesitant opponent would otherwise keep them out), once a lunge has carried them right in. Harder levels raise the player's hit threshold, lower the opponent's and its caution; the arm keeps its length, which would favour the rapier. The opponent's scripts go from plain guard-and-cut patterns (level 0) to parries of the player's line and attacks on the lines he leaves open (levels 2-4). Attack keys advance from afar and strike once in reach; a guard is kept until another key, an attack or step back is one per key press. Edges and flag heights fit the 640x480 sword screen. Tuned by bot fights through flibustier-sim at every level, weapon and crew ratio, with random lunges (the career bot's) and a player who parries the line he sees raised 0.2 s late: with a crew as strong as the enemy's, random lunges win boardings at the two easy levels nearly always and about half at the middle level, the parrying player nine in ten there; at the easiest level boardings are won even outnumbered three to one. Duels are won at the easy and middle levels; at level 3 random lunges win two in three, at level 4 almost none, the parrying player two in three. Over eight career bot careers the bot won 96% of its sword fights, up from 63%. Clean-room note: after these values were final, a search of the docs printed seven lines of the engine's rules spec on the weapons' reach (no game-data numbers); nothing was changed after it.
